Manage versions and revisions

If you want to explore a different direction without losing your current work, tell Claude: “Save what we have and try a completely different approach.” Claude will save your current project and confirm where it’s saved, so you can reference earlier iterations in the conversation easily.

Export and share

Once your design is ready, you can share it with colleagues or export it for use elsewhere. The right format depends on your use case—whether you’re getting stakeholder feedback, handing off to engineering, or presenting to a group.

Use the “Export” button in the upper right corner when viewing your project to choose from the following export formats.

  • Download as .zip
  • Export as PDF
  • Export as PPTX
  • Export to Google Slides
  • Export as standalone HTML
  • Send to the tools you already use: Adobe Experience Manager, Adobe for Creativity, Adobe Journey Optimizer, Base44, Canva, Gamma, HubSpot, Hyperframes, Lovable, Miro, Netlify, Replit, v0, Vercel, and Wix
  • Handoff to Claude Code
    • Send to local coding agent
    • Send to Claude Code Web

Designs start private to you. To share one, click “Share” and choose who can open it and what they can do. People you share a design with can view, comment on, or edit it. Learn more about sharing artifacts.

Usage and pricing

Claude Design counts toward the same usage limits as the rest of Claude. Design activity draws from the same pool as the rest of your work with Claude, including Claude Code, so there’s no separate Claude Design allowance to track. Complex projects with large codebases or many iterations consume more usage.

If you reach your usage limits, Claude Design is unavailable until your limits reset. If you’ve enabled usage credits, you can keep working after reaching your included limits. Learn more about how usage and length limits work.

Note: Claude Design previously had its own weekly allowance, separate from your other usage limits. All Claude Design activity now counts toward your plan’s shared limits.

Tips for best results

  • Import a complete design system. Import a complete design system that includes your styles, fonts, and components.
  • Start simple, then layer in complexity. Begin with the core layout and content, then add interactions, edge cases, and polish. Claude responds well to incremental requests.
  • Be specific in your feedback. “This doesn’t look right” is hard to act on. “Tighten the spacing between form fields to 8px” gives Claude exactly what it needs.
  • Reference your design system. If you know a component exists in your brand’s system, mention it by name: “Use the Primary Button component” or “Apply the Card layout pattern.”
  • Think about responsiveness early. Mention whether your design needs to work on mobile, tablet, and desktop, or just one of those.
  • Ask for variations. If you’re unsure about a direction, ask Claude to show you 2–3 options. Comparing alternatives is much faster than guessing.
  • Ask Claude for feedback. Claude can review your design for accessibility, contrast ratios, information hierarchy, and general usability. Treat it as a design collaborator, not just a generator.

Known limitations

A few things to be aware of:

  • Comment persistence: Inline comments occasionally don’t appear on the page, but you can still see them by opening the comments view.
  • Large codebases: Consider linking very large repositories from Claude Code to avoid lag or browser issues. To sync a design system, use /design-sync from Claude Code.
  • Chat errors: If you hit a “chat upstream error,” try starting a new chat tab within the same project.
  • Mobile: It’s not possible to change sharing settings on the Claude app for iOS and Android, so you’ll need to use Claude on web or desktop for this.
  • Multi-person editing: Two or more people editing a design project at the same time is still basic and may not work reliably.
  • Design system import: Design system import is only as good as its source. A messy codebase or an incomplete file will show up in the output.
  • Version history: Claude Design doesn’t have version history yet.
  • Deleting from the list of layers: In the properties panel’s list of layers, Delete, Backspace, and cut act on what’s selected on the canvas, not the row you moved to. Press Return on the row first.
  • Adding to a design with a keyboard: Placing a new text layer, artboard, shape, or note on the canvas needs a mouse or trackpad. Ask Claude to add it.

Get started with Claude Docs

Claude Docs lets you write living documents with Claude and the people you work with. Ask for a doc in any conversation, and Claude drafts it in front of you, asks clarifying questions up front, and leaves comments explaining its choices. You can edit the doc yourself, ask Claude for the next pass, and share it by link, without moving your work into another tool.

This guide covers creating your first doc, editing it with Claude and your team, and sharing or exporting it when it’s ready.

Create an artifact with Claude

Claude Docs is available on Free, Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise plans, and it’s on by default. On Enterprise plans, it turns on by default on October 15, 2026, and owners can turn it on before then in Organization settings > Artifacts.

How Claude Docs works

A doc is a rich-text document saved to your Claude account. It can include headings, tables, and other formatting, and it can have more than one tab, like sections of a notebook. Every doc you create is saved in the Artifacts tab, so you can find it again from any conversation.

Claude starts from the context it already has. When you ask for a doc, Claude can draw on your files, memory, projects, skills, and the apps you’ve connected, so you don’t start from a blank page.

The person who creates a doc is its owner. Anyone the owner shares it with can view, comment on, or edit it. Claude works on a doc only when a signed-in person asks it to, and it can’t do anything that person doesn’t have permission to do. Every change is attributed to whoever made it, whether that’s a person or Claude.

Create a doc

From a conversation

Ask Claude for a doc in any conversation. For example:

  • “Turn the plan we just worked through into a product spec I can share with the team.”
  • “Draft this week’s status report from my notes and last week’s numbers.”
  • “Write an onboarding guide for new hires from the benefits deck in my Google Drive.”
  • “Pull my notes on this account into a one-page brief for tomorrow’s call.”

Claude asks a few questions before it starts, then drafts the doc on screen. You can also start your request with /docs, or by selecting “Output” then “Docs” from the message box.

From the Artifacts tab
  • Go to the Artifacts tab.
  • Select a Docs template from the gallery.
  • Describe the doc you want.
Where you can create docs

You can ask for a doc wherever you talk to Claude:

  • Claude on web and desktop: Ask in any conversation, or start from the Artifacts tab.
  • Claude Code: Ask Claude to turn the session you’re in into a spec, runbook, or readout. On desktop, the doc opens in the side panel. In the terminal, Claude gives you a link to open the doc on the web.
  • Claude app for iOS and Android: Ask for a doc in any conversation and check back later for the result. Open it from the Artifacts tab to view it full screen. You can also edit a doc.
Tips for better results

A good request says what the doc is for, who will read it, and what it should cover. “A two-page launch brief for our sales team covering pricing, timing, and the top three customer questions” gets you further than “a launch brief.” If the content lives somewhere specific, name the file or connected app Claude should use.

Edit your doc

Nothing is locked while Claude works. You can edit alongside Claude at any time, and the final say is always yours.

Edit directly

Click into the doc and type. Your changes save automatically and appear right away for everyone who has the doc open.

Ask Claude

Ask for changes in the conversation, like “Tighten the intro and add a risks section.” Claude edits the doc and tells you what changed.

Use comments

Select text and leave a comment for your collaborators. To ask Claude for an edit, mention @Claude in a comment. Claude replies in the thread, makes the change, and explains what it did and why. Claude also leaves its own comments while drafting, to explain its choices or ask you a question.

Add charts and visuals

Instead of pasting in screenshots, ask Claude to add a chart, diagram, graph, or timeline to your doc. Claude pulls the data from your connected apps and builds the chart in the doc. Charts and diagrams don’t update on their own, even when the data comes from a connected app like Salesforce or Google Sheets. To refresh one, ask Claude to pull the latest data.

Work on a doc with your team

People with edit access can work on the same doc at the same time as you and Claude, and everyone’s edits appear in real time. Claude always acts with the permissions of the person who asked, so it can’t edit a doc for someone who only has view access.

Use Claude Docs with a keyboard

To get into and out of the artifact panel, see Use artifacts with a keyboard or screen reader. That article also explains what focus means, what to do on a Mac laptop or in Safari, and how shortcuts are written. For the full list of shortcuts, including the keys for tables, images, links, and the list of doc tabs, see Claude Docs keyboard shortcuts.

This section calls a doc’s tabs doc tabs, so they aren’t confused with the Tab key.

Open the list of keyboard shortcuts

Claude Docs lists its own shortcuts. With focus anywhere inside a doc, press Cmd+/ (Ctrl+/ on Windows). It works while you’re typing and in a doc you can only view. When focus isn’t in a text box, ? on its own opens the list too. Escape closes it and puts you back where you were. From the panel’s header, Cmd+/ (Ctrl+/ on Windows) opens the shortcut list for Claude itself, which doesn’t cover artifacts.

Note: On keyboards where / is typed with Shift+7, such as German, Italian, and Nordic layouts, Cmd+/ (Ctrl+/ on Windows) doesn’t open the list: on those keyboards it’s the numbered list shortcut. Press Escape to leave the text, and then press ?.

Move into and out of the text

In a doc’s text, Tab works the way it does in a word processor: it indents a list item, moves to the next table cell, or moves between the title and the body. It doesn’t leave the text.

To move into the text:

  • Press Tab from the panel’s header to reach the doc’s toolbar. If you can only view or comment on the doc and the list of doc tabs is shown beside the text, the toolbar may have no buttons for you, and Tab then goes to that list.
  • Keep pressing Tab. You pass the list of doc tabs, if it’s shown beside the text, and the comments, if the doc has any, and then reach the text. How many presses it takes depends on what the doc contains.

To leave the text:

  • Press Escape. If the formatting toolbar or another pop-up is showing, this closes it.
  • Press Escape again if you need to. Focus moves to the doc tabs button at the start of the doc’s toolbar, which shows the name of the doc tab you’re on. If the list of doc tabs is shown beside the text, the button just says “Tabs”. In a doc you can only view or comment on, there’s no button while the list is shown, and focus moves into the list instead: to the doc tab you’re on, or to the row you were last on.
  • Press Tab to go back toward the text (you pass the list of doc tabs, if it’s shown beside the text and you aren’t already in it, then the comments, if the doc has any), or keep pressing Escape to reach the artifact panel.
Format text

The usual shortcuts work in the text, such as Cmd+B (Ctrl+B on Windows) for bold, and a screen reader announces the result. To use the formatting toolbar instead:

  • Select some text.
  • Press Cmd+F6 (Ctrl+F6 on Windows). Focus moves to the formatting toolbar.
  • Press the Left arrow or Right arrow key to move between its buttons.
  • Press Return or Space to use a button. To open a button’s drop-down, such as text style or list type, press the Down arrow key.
  • Press Escape or Tab to go back to the text. Your selection is kept.

Focus stays in the toolbar after you use a formatting button, so you can apply more than one format. Tab from the text never reaches this toolbar.

In a doc, move to the formatting toolbar with Cmd+F6 (Ctrl+F6 on Windows) before you use its buttons. If your screen reader’s own cursor lands on the toolbar another way, some of its buttons, such as “Comment” and “Link,” ask you to press the shortcut first.

Comment in a doc

To add a comment:

  • Select the text you want to comment on.
  • Press Cmd+Option+M (Ctrl+Alt+M on Windows). The “Add a comment” box opens with focus in it.
  • Type your comment. Shift+Return makes a new line, and @ mentions someone.
  • Press Return to post. Focus moves to your new comment.

Press Escape in the box to discard the draft and go back to the text with your selection kept. Where Claude is available in the doc, a “Send to Claude” checkbox comes before the send button. It starts selected, and after that it stays the way you last left it in that doc.

To read the comments on a doc, press Escape to leave the text, and then press Tab until you reach them (if the list of doc tabs is shown beside the text, you pass it first).

What you reach depends on how wide the panel is:

  • Beside a conversation, the panel is usually narrow, and comments show as icons in the margin. Each press of Tab moves to the next icon, and Return opens it. Comments also show as icons in a doc whose page width is set to Wide, and when the list of doc tabs beside the text leaves no room for them.
  • Otherwise, in a wider panel, comments sit beside the text, and Tab moves onto them once. Press the Down arrow or Up arrow key to move between them, and Return or Space to open one.

In an open comment, Return moves into its reply field, and Escape closes it.

Share a doc

Docs start private to you. Share a doc the way you share any artifact: open it and click “Share.” Learn more about sharing artifacts.

A few things are different for docs:

  • Access levels: People you share a doc with can view, comment on, or edit it. Viewers can read the doc. Commenters can read and comment on it. Editors can read, edit, comment on, and export it.
  • Outside your organization: Where your plan and your organization’s settings allow it, you can invite people by email or turn on “Anyone with the link.” People you invite sign in to Claude with the address you invited. People who use the link sign in to Claude and can only view the doc. Free plans can’t send invitations, and email invitations are off by default on Enterprise plans.
  • People you invite from outside your organization: They can ask their own Claude to work on the doc, within the access you gave them. Learn more about what people you invite can do.
  • Renaming and deleting: Only the owner can rename or delete a doc.
Who you can share with
  • Team and Enterprise plans: Invite specific people or a group, or share with everyone in your organization. You can also share outside your organization when an Owner allows it.
  • Free, Pro, Max, and Ultra plans: Share with anyone who has the link. On Pro, Max, and Ultra plans, you can also invite people by email.

Opening a shared doc requires a Claude account.

Access levels
  • Viewers can read the doc.
  • Commenters can read and comment on the doc.
  • Editors can read, edit, comment on, and export the doc.

Only the owner can rename or delete a doc.

Important: Deleting a doc is permanent. There’s no trash, and the doc becomes unavailable to everyone you shared it with after you delete it.

Export a doc

To export a doc, click “Export” and choose a format:

  • Word (.docx)
  • PDF (.pdf)
  • Markdown (.md)
  • Google Docs

You can also ask Claude to turn a doc into a presentation with Claude Slides.

Usage

Claude Docs counts toward your plan’s usage limits, like the rest of your work with Claude. Larger requests, like drafting a long doc from several sources, use more of your limit than a typical message. Learn more about how usage and length limits work.

Turn on Claude Docs for your organization

This section is for Owners and Primary Owners on Team and Enterprise plans.

Owners turn Claude Docs on or off in Organization settings > Artifacts. On Enterprise plans, owners can also limit it to specific groups with custom roles. Learn more in the Artifacts admin guide for Team and Enterprise plans, which also covers offboarding and the Compliance API.

Current limitations

A few things to be aware of:

  • Version history: When the artifact panel is too narrow to show version history beside the text, version history opens over the text, and Tab from the doc’s toolbar doesn’t reach it yet.
  • Charts and diagrams: Charts and diagrams don’t update automatically. Ask Claude to pull the latest data from your connected apps.
  • Compliance logging: Activity inside a doc, like edits and comments, isn’t recorded in the Compliance API yet.
  • Mobile: You can’t change sharing settings in the Claude app for iOS and Android.
  • VoiceOver and typing: In Chrome versions 150 to 152, and in Claude Desktop, VoiceOver doesn’t read text as you type or move through it in a doc. Use Chrome 153 or later. Safari works for docs too.

Get started with Claude Science

Claude Science is Anthropic’s desktop app for scientific research, currently in beta.

Claude Science is available in beta for Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise plans; on Team and Enterprise plans, an Owner or Primary Owner must first turn it on in Organization settings > Claude Science, except on the Claude Team plan for scientists, where it’s on by default.

The Claude Science app runs on macOS 13 or later, Windows 11 (x64), and Linux x64.

Claude Science pairs Claude with a research and analysis environment on your computer: you describe a research task in plain language, and Claude writes and runs code in a sandbox, reads the folders you give it, pulls data from scientific databases through connectors, connects to your own compute clusters, performs long data analyses, and saves results as versioned artifacts with a full provenance record.

For installation, sign-in help, admin controls, what’s not available yet, and the changelog, refer to our documentation on Claude Docs: Claude Science.

To download the app, visit our Claude Science product page.

Get started with Claude Sheets

Claude Sheets is a spreadsheet built into Claude. Ask for a tracker, budget, or model, and Claude builds a working sheet that you, your team, and Claude can edit together. This guide covers creating a sheet, working in it with Claude, importing and exporting data, and sharing it.

Claude Sheets is available in beta on Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise plans. It’s on by default on Team plans. On Enterprise plans, it’s off by default until it’s turned on in Organization settings > Artifacts.

How Claude Sheets works

A sheet is an artifact that you and Claude edit in the same cells. Claude can add tabs, write formulas that work across tabs, apply formatting and conditional formatting, and add dropdowns, checkboxes, and charts. Formulas stay in the cells, so you can see and check how each number was calculated.

When Claude changes a sheet, each edit is outlined as it lands, so you can see what changed. When other people are in the sheet, you all work in the same cells at the same time.

Every sheet you create is saved in the Artifacts tab. Learn more about artifacts and how to use them.

How Claude Sheets differs from Claude for Excel

Claude Sheets puts a spreadsheet inside Claude. Claude for Excel and Claude for Google Workspace bring Claude to the files you already keep in those apps.

Use Claude Sheets for a light, shared sheet that you build with Claude. When your file already lives in Excel or Google Sheets, or you need the full set of features in those apps, use Claude for Excel or Claude for Google Workspace, or export your sheet.

Create a sheet

From a chat

Ask Claude for a sheet in any chat. For example:

  • “Build a campaign tracker with owners, dates, and status.”
  • “Make a hiring budget by team and quarter.”
  • “Forecast next quarter from these deals and flag what’s at risk.”
From the Artifacts tab
  • Go to the Artifacts tab.
  • Select the “Sheets” tile.
  • Describe the sheet you want, or start with a blank sheet.
Tips for better results

Say what the sheet is for and what you want to track. If you already have the numbers, give them to Claude so the sheet is built from your own data.

Work in your sheet

  • Ask Claude: Ask for changes, like “Add a column for budget remaining” or “Highlight anything that’s overdue.”
  • Ask about a range: Select cells and ask Claude about them, like “Why is this total higher than last month?”
  • Edit directly: Type in cells, write formulas, and format your data yourself.
  • Comment: Add comments on cells for your team.

Undo Claude’s changes

Version history shows earlier versions of a sheet and can restore an earlier version, which also removes edits made after it.

Import and export

To bring data into a sheet, you can:

  • Import a CSV file
  • Import from Google Sheets
  • Import from Excel
  • Start from a blank sheet

Pasting from Excel or Google Sheets is also available. To download a sheet, export it as an .xlsx or CSV file. To continue working in another tool, use “Send to.”

Share a sheet

Sheets start private to you. To share one, open it and click “Share.” People you share it with who have “Can edit” access can work on it alongside you and Claude. Learn more about sharing artifacts.

Usage

Claude Sheets counts toward your plan’s usage limits, like the rest of your work with Claude. Learn more about how usage and length limits work.

Turn on Claude Sheets for your organization

This section is for Owners and Primary Owners on Team and Enterprise plans.

Turn Claude Sheets on or off in Organization settings > Artifacts, under Templates. It’s on by default on Team plans and off by default on Enterprise plans. Artifacts must also be on for your organization. On Enterprise plans, once Claude Sheets is on, custom roles can limit it to specific groups. Learn more in the Artifacts admin guide for Team and Enterprise plans.

Current limitations

Claude Sheets is in beta and covers common spreadsheet work. We’re adding more over time.

  • Size: A sheet can hold at least 200,000 filled cells.
  • Charts: Bar, line, and pie charts are available, as well as a wide range of other chart types Claude can generate.
  • Features not available yet: Pivot tables, protected ranges, shared filter views, multi-select dropdowns, and PDF export.
  • Excel features not supported: Macros, VBA, Power Query, DAX, and print layout.
  • Live data: Sheets can’t pull live data from connected apps, and docs, decks, and dashboards can’t use a sheet as a data source.
  • Platforms: Web and desktop are supported, with limited access on mobile.
  • Data controls: Claude Sheets is a beta product, so HIPAA and ZDR are not yet supported.

Get started with Claude Whiteboards

Claude Whiteboards is a shared board for thinking through ideas with Claude. Talk, type, or sketch, and Claude organizes your ideas into diagrams, flows, and groups on the board. This guide covers starting a whiteboard, working on it with Claude and your team, using it in a call, and turning it into a doc or deck.

Claude Whiteboards is available in beta on Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise plans on web, Claude Desktop, and Claude Mobile. It’s on by default on Team plans. On Enterprise plans, it’s off by default until it’s turned on in Organization settings > Artifacts.

Claude Whiteboards isn’t available in Claude for Teachers yet.

How Claude Whiteboards works

A whiteboard is an artifact that you, your team, and Claude work on together. Claude draws what you describe using shapes, arrows, and sections, and anyone on the board can rearrange what’s there.

A board is useful before you know what the final version should be: planning a launch, laying out the options for a decision, or running a retro. When the structure is settled, Claude can turn the board into a doc or deck.

Every whiteboard you create is saved in the Artifacts tab. Learn more about artifacts and how to use them.

Start a whiteboard

From a chat

Ask Claude for a whiteboard in any chat. For example:

  • “Start a whiteboard to plan our product launch.”
  • “Put the options for this decision on a whiteboard, with the trade-offs of each.”
  • “Map this process on a whiteboard from start to finish.”
From the Artifacts tab
  • Go to the Artifacts tab.
  • Select the Whiteboards tile. The tile is labeled “Whiteboard.”
  • Describe what you want to work through, or dictate it into the chat box and send it.

Say it out loud

Dictate a brain dump, like a plan, a list of options, or a messy process. Claude groups related ideas, puts steps in order, and connects the ones that depend on each other. You can also type or sketch. To dictate, select the microphone next to the send button in the chat box. To stop, select the microphone again or press Escape, and your words stay in the box. Select the send button or press Return to send them to Claude.

Dictation follows your browser’s language and works in Amharic, Chinese (Simplified), Czech, Danish, Dutch, English, French, German, Greek, Hebrew, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Swahili, Swedish, Thai, Turkish, and Ukrainian.

Work on the board with Claude

  • Reorganize the board: Ask Claude to regroup the board by theme or turn it into a timeline.
  • Find the gaps: Ask what’s missing between two steps. Claude adds its suggestions to the board for you to check.
  • Focus on one area: Drag across a region of the board to ask Claude about just that part.

Work on it together

Everyone on a board works on it live and can rearrange what’s there. To see what a teammate is looking at, follow them around the board.

To bring people onto a board, open it and click “Share.” People outside your organization can join if you invite them by email. On Team and Enterprise plans, Email invitations outside your organization needs to be on in Organization settings > Artifacts. Learn more about sharing artifacts.

Turn your board into something else

When the thinking is done, ask Claude to turn the board into a doc or deck. For example: “Turn this board into a project plan.” To continue working in another tool, use “Send to.” You can send a board to Lucid, Miro, and Zoho Vani, and we’re adding more over time. To save a board as a file, click “Share,” go to “Export,” and choose PNG. You can add pictures and videos to a board, but you can’t import a board from a file.

Usage

Claude Whiteboards counts toward your plan’s usage limits, like the rest of your work with Claude.

Learn more about how usage and length limits work.

Current limitations

Claude Whiteboards is in beta. At launch:

  • Connected apps: Claude works from what’s on the board and doesn’t use context from your connected apps.
  • Data controls: Claude Whiteboards isn’t available to organizations with HIPAA-ready configurations. In organizations with zero data retention for Claude Code, it’s available in chat and Cowork, isn’t covered by zero data retention, and isn’t available in Claude Code.

How to create custom skills

Skills are available for users on Free, Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise plans. This feature requires code execution to be enabled. Skills are also available in beta for Claude Code users and for all API users using the code execution tool.

Custom skills let you enhance Claude with specialized knowledge and workflows specific to your organization or personal work style. This article explains how to create, structure, and test your own skills.

Skills can be as simple as a few lines of instructions or as complex as multi-file packages with executable code. The best skills:

  • Solve a specific, repeatable task
  • Have clear instructions that Claude can follow
  • Include examples when helpful
  • Define when they should be used
  • Are focused on one workflow rather than trying to do everything

Record a skill

Recording a skill is available on Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans, in Cowork in Claude for Mac. It isn’t available in chat, on Windows, or on Free and Enterprise plans.

Instead of writing a skill by hand, you can record yourself doing a task and let Claude build the skill from what it observes. You send Claude a video of your screen, clicks, typing, and voice, and Claude proposes a skill for you to review before you save it.

Before you record
  • Update to the latest version of Claude for Mac.
  • Grant the macOS permissions Claude asks for the first time you record: Accessibility for mouse and keyboard tracking, and Screen recording for screen visibility. macOS may ask you to restart Claude.
  • Close any files, apps, or conversations you don’t want captured.

Warning: Don’t type passwords or secrets, or display sensitive information or private conversations while recording. Everything on your screen is captured for the length of the session, along with anything you say.

Record your workflow
  • Open Cowork in Claude for Mac.
  • Start a recording one of two ways:
    • Click the “+” button in the composer, then select “Record a skill.”
    • Go to Customize > Skills, click “Add,” then select “Record your screen.”
  • Click “Start recording.” To narrate as you work, leave the microphone on. Use the microphone control to mute it or choose a different input.
  • Do the task the way you normally would. The capture bar shows that recording is in progress and counts the steps it’s captured.
  • Click “Done” when you’re finished, or “Discard” to throw the recording away without creating anything.

A recording can run for about 10 minutes. A countdown appears in the capture bar when you have about a minute left. When it reaches zero, recording stops and everything you’ve captured up to that point is sent to Claude, the same as if you’d clicked “Done.”

Tip: Talk through what you’re doing while you record. Narration gives Claude context it can’t get from your screen alone, like why you skip a step or how you choose between two options.

What happens after you click Done

Claude starts a Cowork task and reviews the recording, then proposes a skill. Depending on what it finds, you’ll see one of two things:

  • A new skill, marked NEW on the proposal card. Click “Save” to keep it, or “Dismiss” to discard the proposal.
  • An update to an existing skill. If the recording overlaps a skill you already have, Claude proposes changes to that skill instead. The card shows which skill the proposal is based on. Click “Update” to apply the changes, or “Dismiss” to discard them.

Expand Content on the proposal card to read the skill before you decide.

Skills you save from a recording appear in Customize > Skills and work like any other skill. You can edit them, share them, and delete them on the same terms.

What’s kept from a recording

The video and audio from your recording aren’t retained. After you send your recording to Claude, Claude reviews the recording to build the skill. What’s saved afterward is a set of screenshots from the session, which you can view by expanding the Recorded demonstration step in the task.

Because those screenshots live in the Cowork task, deleting the task removes them. See Get started with Claude Cowork for how task deletion and retention work.

Create a skill.md file

Every skill consists of a directory containing at minimum a skill.md file, which is the core of the skill. This file must start with a YAML frontmatter to hold name and description fields, which are required metadata. It can also contain additional metadata, instructions for Claude or reference files, executable scripts, or tools.

Required metadata fields

name: A human-friendly name for your skill (64 characters maximum)

  • Example: Brand Guidelines

description: A clear description of what the skill does and when to use it.

  • This is critical—Claude uses this to determine when to invoke your skill (200 characters maximum).
  • Example: Apply Acme Corp brand guidelines to presentations and documents, including official colors, fonts, and logo usage.
Optional metadata fields

dependencies: Software packages required by your skill.

  • Example: python>=3.8, pandas>=1.5.0

The metadata in the skill.md file serves as the first level of a progressive disclosure system, providing just enough information for Claude to know when the skill should be used without having to load all of the content.

Markdown body

The markdown body is the second level of detail after the metadata, so Claude will access this if needed after reading the metadata. Depending on your task, Claude can access the skill.md file and use the skill.

Example skill.md

Brand guidelines skill

## Metadata
name: Brand Guidelines
description: Apply Acme Corp brand guidelines to all presentations and documents

## Overview
This skill provides Acme Corp's official brand guidelines for creating consistent, professional materials. When creating presentations, documents, or marketing materials, apply these standards to ensure all outputs match Acme's visual identity. Claude should reference these guidelines whenever creating external-facing materials or documents that represent Acme Corp.

## Brand Colors

Our official brand colors are:
- Primary: #FF6B35 (Coral)
- Secondary: #004E89 (Navy Blue)
- Accent: #F7B801 (Gold)
- Neutral: #2E2E2E (Charcoal)

## Typography

Headers: Montserrat Bold
Body text: Open Sans Regular
Size guidelines:
- H1: 32pt
- H2: 24pt
- Body: 11pt

## Logo Usage

Always use the full-color logo on light backgrounds. Use the white logo on dark backgrounds. Maintain minimum spacing of 0.5 inches around the logo.

## When to Apply

Apply these guidelines whenever creating:
- PowerPoint presentations
- Word documents for external sharing
- Marketing materials
- Reports for clients

## Resources

See the resources folder for logo files and font downloads.

Add resources

If you have too much information to add to a single skill.md file (e.g., sections that only apply to specific scenarios), you can add more content by adding files within your skill directory. For example, add a REFERENCE.md file containing supplemental and reference information to your skill directory. Referencing it in skill.md will help Claude decide if it needs to access that resource when executing the skill.

Add scripts

For more advanced skills, attach executable code files to skill.md, allowing Claude to run code. For example, our document skills use the following programming languages and packages:

  • Python (pandas, numpy, matplotlib)
  • JavaScript/Node.js
  • Packages to help with file editing
  • Visualization tools

Note: Claude and Claude Code can install packages from standard repositories (Python PyPI, JavaScript npm) when loading skills. It’s not possible to install additional packages at runtime with API Skills—all dependencies must be pre-installed in the container.

Package your skill

Once your skill folder is complete:

  • Ensure the folder name matches your skill’s name.
  • Create a ZIP file of the folder.
  • The ZIP should contain the skill folder as its root (not a subfolder).

Correct structure:

my-skill.zip

└── my-skill/

├── skill.md

└── resources/

Incorrect structure:

my-skill.zip

└── (files directly in ZIP root)

Test your skill

Before uploading

  1. Review your skill.md for clarity.

  2. Check that the description accurately reflects when Claude should use the skill.

  3. Verify all referenced files exist in the correct locations.

  4. Test with example prompts to ensure Claude invokes it appropriately.

After uploading to Claude

  1. Enable the skill in Customize > Skills.

  2. Try several different prompts that should trigger it.

  3. Review Claude’s thinking to confirm it’s loading the skill.

  4. Iterate on the description if Claude isn’t using it when expected.

When you’re iterating on a skill with Claude in chat, you can edit the skill files directly where they open beside the conversation. Highlight the text you want changed, click “Edit with Claude,” and type your request. For skills with multiple files, leave edit requests across the files and send them together, and Claude applies them in one pass. Learn more about editing artifacts.

Note for Team and Enterprise plans: To make a skill available to all users in your organization, see Provision and manage skills for your organization.

Best practices

Keep it focused: Create separate skills for different workflows. Multiple focused skills compose better than one large skill.

Write clear descriptions: Claude uses descriptions to decide when to invoke your skill. Be specific about when it applies.

Start simple: Begin with basic instructions in Markdown before adding complex scripts. You can always expand on the skill later.

Use examples: Include example inputs and outputs in your skill.md file to help Claude understand what success looks like.

Test incrementally: Test after each significant change rather than building a complex skill all at once.

Skills can build on each other: While skills can’t explicitly reference other skills, Claude can use multiple skills together automatically. This composability is one of the most powerful parts of the skills feature.

Review the open Agent Skills specification: Follow the guidelines at agentskills.io, so skills you create can work across platforms that adopt the standard.

For a more in-depth guide to skill creation, refer to Skill authoring best practices in our Claude Docs.

Security considerations

  • Exercise caution when adding scripts to your skill.md file.
  • Don’t hardcode sensitive information (API keys, passwords).
  • Review any skills you download before enabling them.
  • Use appropriate MCP connections for external service access.

Example skills to reference

Visit our repository on GitHub for example skills you can use as templates: github.com.

Manage plugins, skills, and connectors from one Plugins page

Plugins, skills, and connectors are coming together in one Plugins experience. This article explains what’s changing, which accounts are affected, and what you need to do. Most organizations don’t need to do anything.

This change reaches Enterprise plans on November 30, 2026. Free, Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans start rolling out on October 29.

What’s changing

You’ll find, add, and manage plugins, skills, and connectors from one place. In the sidebar, what was previously Customize becomes Plugins, and one Plugins page replaces the separate Skills, Connectors, and Plugins tabs in Claude.

For users
  • New name: Customize now reads Plugins in the sidebar, the chat menu, and settings.
  • Your plugins first: Your plugins appear above the plugins you can browse. It includes plugins from your organization and plugins shared with you.
  • Quick filters: You can narrow the list to skills or connectors. Each card shows which type it is.
  • One detail page: Plugins and connectors open on the same page layout.
  • Directory labels: Public plugins show Verified or Community.
  • Skills work as plugins: To use a skill, click the “+” button or type “/” in chat. You can still share skills.

Your existing connectors, skills, and plugins stay installed. Removing a plugin that packages skills and a connector doesn’t disconnect its connector, so you’ll need to disconnect it separately.

For admins
  • Your controls: Most existing controls stay in place, with the changes below. Plugin and connector controls stay mostly separate in Organization settings.
  • Plugins and connectors keep separate pages: In Organization settings, Plugins & skills and Connectors become one Plugins group, with separate pages for plugins, connectors, policy, marketplaces, and requests.
  • Skills disabled setting: Starting November 30, if Skills are disabled for your organization, plugins are also blocked in the Claude Desktop app. This matches how Claude web and Claude Code work today.

Which accounts are affected

The timing depends on your plan.

Plan

When the change reaches you

Free, Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans

Rolling out gradually starting October 29, generally available November 9.

Enterprise plan

On by default starting November 30

The Skills-off rule applies to Team and Enterprise plans starting November 30.

What you need to do

Most users don’t need to do anything. You will continue to be able to use your existing connectors, skills, and plugins that are already installed on your account.

Admins of organizations with Skills turned off need to turn on Skills before November 30 to keep plugins in Claude Desktop.

If you’re a user

No action is needed. To find what you’ve already added:

  • Click Plugins in the sidebar.
  • Open Your plugins > Show all.
  • Use the quick filters to show plugins that only contain skills or connectors.
If you’re an admin on a Team or Enterprise plan

No action is needed if Skills are enabled for your organization.

If Skills are disabled for your organization, Plugins will stop working in Claude Desktop with this update given that Skills will become packaged into Plugins. Before November 30, choose whether to keep Plugins working on Claude Desktop:

  • To keep plugins available: Turn on Skills.
    • Note: This will be renamed to Plugins on November 30.
  • To block plugins: Leave Skills off. Plugins stop working in Claude Cowork and the Code tab starting November 30.

To enable Plugins, you’ll need to be an owner:

  • Go to Organization settings > Library > Policy. Turn on Cloud code execution and file creation if it’s off. Plugins require it.
  • Turn on Skills.
    • Note: This will be renamed to Plugins on November 30.

Important: If your organization uses the HIPAA configuration, your BAA doesn’t cover connectors, plugins, or skills, including after an owner turns them on. Keep protected health information (PHI) out of them.

Move from standalone Claude Design to Claude

Claude Design now lives in Claude. The standalone Claude Design site (claude.ai/design) will close on December 14, 2026, and you can still access it until that date. This article explains what’s changing and when, how to move your design systems today, and what happens to your projects.

Claude Design is available on Free, Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise plans.

What’s changing and when

You can keep using the standalone version until it closes on December 14, 2026. Move or download your projects before then.

When you start a new design, design system, or slide deck in Claude, it’s created as an artifact.

What happens to your work

When you move a design system, the original stays in the standalone version. Your chats and comments can’t move to Claude, so they stay in the standalone version until it closes.

Important: Design systems that have already moved become read-only for everyone in the standalone version as soon as Move to Claude is available to your organization. If you’ve kept editing one there, those changes didn’t move, so make them again in Claude.

What you need to do

  • Move your design systems now.
  • On Team and Enterprise plans, ask your organization’s owner to set a default design system to get the most out of artifacts.
  • Move the projects you want to keep. See What happens to your projects.
  • If you’re a Team or Enterprise owner, check that artifacts and design systems are turned on. On Enterprise plans, design systems are off by default.

Move your design systems

Note: Once Move to Claude is available to your organization, design systems no longer have their own move. They move the same way as projects. Each design system’s owner can move it, or an owner of your organization can move everything at once. See What happens to your projects.

Before you start
  • One move brings over every design system in your organization, including other people’s, so it only needs to be started once.
  • Anyone who can use Claude Design can start it, not just your organization’s owners.
  • Each design system keeps its owner and the people it’s shared with. If the owner has left your organization, the Primary Owner becomes its owner.
  • Empty design systems aren’t moved, and neither are ones made from a built-in starter theme, even if you’ve edited them.

Important: Published design systems that aren’t private will be shared with everyone in your organization and appear in their design system menu. On individual plans, nothing is shared.

Start the move
  • Open the Artifacts page in Claude.
  • Click “Move team design systems” in the “Claude Design lives here now” banner. If you’ve closed the banner, choose it from the Claude Design menu. To open the menu, click the “…” button on the Design tile under “Make something new.” If there’s no Design tile, click the “…” button at the top right of the page.
  • Click “Move” to confirm. On individual plans, there’s no confirmation step, and the move starts right away.
  • Wait for the move to finish. If you close the window, it keeps running.
  • Check the results. Under Moved, the window lists each design system with its owner’s name and an “Open” link. You’ll see only the design systems you have access to, unless you’re an owner of your organization.

After the move

Your moved design systems appear in the design system menu when you make designs and slide decks in Claude. To see them all, choose “View design systems” from the Claude Design menu on the Artifacts page. The list opens in Settings.

Owners can set your organization’s default design system here. Open a design system’s menu and choose “Set as default.” Click a design system’s name to open it.

A moved design system keeps its files as they were, and you can’t edit it yourself on its page yet. Its editors see a note at the top saying that it was moved and that they can ask Claude to make changes.

Learn more about getting started with Claude Design.

If a design system can’t move

The window lists it under Didn’t move, with its name, owner, and a short reason, such as “it’s too large.”

To reopen the results later, click the count in the banner on the Artifacts page, such as “6 of your 11 design systems couldn’t move.”

Anyone who can edit the design system can fix problems with its own files or size. If you can’t edit it, you won’t be able to run the check, so ask its owner, who’s named in the row.

To fix a design system:

  • Click “Fix in Claude Design Standalone” in its row.
  • Click “Check” on the Check whether this design system can move to Claude card.
  • Fix the files the check lists, using the table below.
  • Click “Check again” until it says “Nothing found in the way.”
  • Move again from the Artifacts page in Claude.

What the check says

What to do

Too large for an artifact

Shrink or remove them

With a name an artifact can’t use

Rename them

A kind an artifact can’t hold

Convert or remove them

Can’t go in a design system artifact

Remove them

Can’t be opened

Save them again, or remove them

With characters that can’t be read

Fix or remove them

Contents missing

Upload them again, or remove them

If the whole design system is too large, the card says “It’s too large. Make it smaller.” instead of listing files. Remove files you don’t need, then check again.

Note: The uploads folder often contains duplicate files, so it’s an easy place to start trimming down a design system.

Some reasons need your organization’s owner to fix them: “design systems are turned off for your team,” “your team can’t publish artifacts,” or “its owner’s role doesn’t include design systems.” The first two stop the move, and any design systems it hadn’t started are listed under Not started. Once they’re fixed, move again.

Sometimes the card says “Can’t move this design system” without saying why. If this happens, click “Download design system” to keep a copy of its files. You can click “Check again” later, and if it still can’t move, let us know. See Get help.

Move again

Note: Once Move to Claude is available to your organization, this section no longer applies. A later move doesn’t update a design system that has already moved. To replace it with a fresh copy, its owner deletes it in Claude, then moves it again from the standalone version.

To move new, changed, or fixed design systems, choose “Move again” from the Claude Design menu on the Artifacts page. To reopen your last results, choose “View last move,” just below it.

When you move again:

If the design system is

What happens

New, or changed in the standalone version since the last move

It’s moved

Unchanged in both places

It’s left alone and marked “already moved”

Changed in Claude since it was moved

It’s listed under Skipped as “changed on claude.ai, left as they are,” so your edits in Claude aren’t overwritten

To replace a moved design system with a fresh copy, delete it in Claude, then move again. To keep any changes you’ve made to it, duplicate it first.

What happens to your projects

Until they’re moved, your projects stay in the standalone version and keep working until it closes. The Artifacts page in Claude also lists up to 60 of them, and they open in the standalone version.

When you move a project to Claude, it becomes an artifact.

  • On Team and Enterprise plans, artifacts also need to be on for your organization. On Enterprise plans with custom roles, your role needs them too.
  • Organizations with customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) can move individual projects, lists of projects, design systems, or everything at once. Standalone Claude Design doesn’t support CMEK, so its data won’t be encrypted under your key until you move. Once a project moves to Claude, it’s encrypted under your key.
  • Organizations with the HIPAA-ready configuration can move projects once an owner turns on Artifacts and Design. Moved projects and design systems aren’t covered under your Business Associate Agreement (BAA), so keep protected health information (PHI) out of them. See For Team and Enterprise owners.
  • Organizations with zero data retention (ZDR) for Claude Code can move projects once an owner turns on artifacts. ZDR doesn’t cover artifacts. If artifacts stay off there, download your projects before the standalone version closes.

To move a project:

  • Open the project in the standalone version at claude.ai/design. Only the project’s owner can move it.
  • Start the review from the pop-up or from the banner at the top of the project.
  • Read the review. It lists what moves, anything that will work differently, and what stays behind. You can also download a copy as a .zip file. Then confirm the move.
  • Keep the tab open until the move finishes.
  • Open the project in Claude. It’s now an artifact on the Artifacts page.

After the move, the copy in the standalone version is read-only for everyone, and this can’t be undone. Your chats and comments stay in that copy, where you can read them until the standalone version closes. Sharing carries over where Claude supports it.

You can also move all of your own projects at once, or only the ones you choose. On Team and Enterprise plans, your organization’s owners can move everyone’s projects at once with “Move everything.”

“Move everything” moves templates and design systems too. Only an Owner or the Primary Owner can start it, not an Admin. To start it:

  • Open the Artifacts page in Claude. If you belong to more than one claude.ai organization, make sure the right one is selected first.
  • Click “Move” in the “Claude Design lives here now” banner. If you’ve closed the banner, click the “…” button on the Design tile and choose “Move from standalone.”
  • In the window that opens, choose “Move everything.” If a move of everything has already run and some items were left behind, the option reads “Move what’s left.”

If you don’t see “Move everything,” check that you’re an Owner or the Primary Owner, and that Claude Design and Artifacts are both turned on in Organization settings.

Most projects keep their owner, and private projects stay private. If a project’s owner has left your organization, it goes to an owner of your organization, usually the Primary Owner, and Claude shows that person a list called “Projects moved to you.” Anything that can’t move stays in the standalone version, and the results say why. Before December 14, 2026, download anything that can’t move. As with any move, the standalone copies of moved projects become read-only for everyone.

Important: If your organization has a retention period that covers artifacts, a project or design system that moves, or has already moved, to Claude can be permanently deleted if nobody opens it for that period. The period starts on the day of the move and restarts when someone opens or edits the artifact. Learn more in Configure custom data retention controls for Enterprise plans.

What isn’t carried over

These stay in the standalone version and are deleted some time after it closes, per our data retention practices:

  • Your chats with Claude
  • Comments on your projects and design systems

Pages you published with “Publish as artifact” are artifacts in Claude, so closing the standalone version doesn’t affect their links. Temporary public links expire on their own in about an hour.

Important: Save anything you need from your chats and comments before the standalone version closes.

For Team and Enterprise owners

Claude Design in Claude depends on artifacts. If artifacts are off for your organization, people can’t create designs in Claude or move anything, and they won’t see the “Claude Design lives here now” banner.

To check your settings, navigate to Organization settings > Artifacts:

Setting

What it’s for

Default

Artifacts

Everything below depends on it

Moving design systems and creating new ones

On for Team plans, off for Enterprise plans
